units.unit: The student is investigating Hong Kong's subdivided flats and the rent control debate.
The student wants to understand what has actually been tried and what the evidence says.
The student wants to start with the problem itself and whether a cap has actually been tried.
The student asks what the current Hong Kong ordinance covers.
The student asks whether any rent cap has been tried somewhere comparable.
The student says all five sources cover problem definition, Hong Kong data, comparative cases and the counter-view.
The student says the working paper showed hard caps shrink stock while cap-on-increase rules barely do.
The student says a legal source said a rate-style band is easier to defend than a flat cap.
The student says the consultation piece pointed toward a band.
The student combined those sources to land on the recommendation.
The student says the working paper's elasticity figures and modelled finding that 3,000–4,000 households a year would be shut out told them who bears the cost of contraction.
The student says D1's tenant profile told them those excluded households are the same people the policy is meant to help.
The student says the cap protects current tenants at the expense of the next ones, a tension none of the sources states outright.
The student says D1 describes how the 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within an existing tenancy but left the initial rent untouched.
The student says they pulled the detail in when building the argument that the status quo fails tenants at the point where rents are set.
The student says the point came from document D2, cited as [D2p2].
The student says they put it in paragraph 3 because it supports the claim that the ordinance failed at the initial rent.
The student says the figure came from D2 [D2p2], which reports real rent burden rising from 31 to 34 percent.
The student says it was a new detail added when building the paragraph showing the ordinance didn't help tenants at the point that matters.
